intro.body:
*You slept only at the mercy of cruel dreams. Your room is dark. But no—This isn’t your room. There’s no window or lamp or bed. You’re lying on rock, fully dressed, and your clothes are soggy.*

*Why can’t you remember? This has happened before. In a strange house. At a hotel. On the road.*

*But none of that fits. Then you remember a woman you were with. But why would she throw you in the sea? Because that seems to be where you are.*

*You can smell it. You can taste the salt on your lips. You can feel it: you’re soaking in icy, moving water.*

*It’s time for you to stand up. When you do, you hit your head. You crouch and light a match you find in a happily dry matchbook in your pocket.*

*The tiny fire shows you a cave. You’re in a shallow pool. Every surface is slick. Slime glitters on the encircling black walls. The carcasses of fish, former captives of the tides, linger here and there. One is caught between jutting spurs of rock. You don’t want to end like that. Set in part of the ceiling is a metal hatch. Panicking, you bang on it. Silence. Then—muffled and coming from the other side—a plaintive, inhuman sound. You stop banging. You don’t like this.*

*The seawater has a gentle current. The carcass between the spurs comes loose and begins to float in it.*

flashback1.intro: *“So that’s the story. The first thing we have to do is go to Innsmouth and find Agent Elina Harper. I haven’t heard from her since the 5*th*,” Thomas Dawson told you.*
flashback1.silasMarsh:
*“Innsmouth,” you repeated. “I thought that might be why you wanted me.”*

*“I know you left Innsmouth a long time ago,” Dawson said, “but you have roots there. Your connections might help our investigation.”*

*“I don’t know any of those folks,” you said. “I tried hard to forget them. I tried hard to forget the town.”*

*“I know. But you have the name. You have the— pedigree. We need your help. Besides, we know about your dreams.”*
flashback1.veteran:
*“So, Uncle Sam wants me to go to Innsmouth. Why me?” you asked.*

*“We were both in the war,” Dawson said. “That sets us apart from most people. But what sets us apart even more—What we saw. What we’ve seen. You know what’s out there.”*

*“No, I don’t know,” you said, wondering what he meant. “You don’t either.”*

*“But I do know about your dreams,” said Dawson.*
flashback1.mystic:
*“I suppose you reached out to me because you’ve heard of my—gifts,” you said.*

*“Gifts? Is that what they are?” asked Dawson. “Not what I’d like to find under the Christmas tree. But yes, that’s right. We know about you. But that’s not all—We know about your dreams.”*
flashback1.agency:
*“I understand that you requested my help,” you said, “and I know your commitments won’t allow you to disclose why you find the tip you mentioned so—ominous. I understand why intelligence isn’t shared between our organizations, that we work in parallel. But if we’re going to be working together on* this *mission—”*

*Dawson shook his head. “No. Can’t do it. You’ll learn on the job.”*

*“I insist—”*

*“Agent, we know about your dreams,” Dawson said.*

*Your blood ran cold. For once, you didn’t know what to say.*

*“They make you a liability for your own organization,” he continued. “Or they will.”*
flashback1.rest:
*“What does this have to do with my dreams?” you asked.*

*“I can’t disclose that. And frankly, I don’t fully know. We believe there* is *a connection.”*

*“You’re asking a lot for the sake of mere belief.”*

*“I can say this: It’s clear you’re psychically sensitive to what’s happening in Innsmouth. The dreams you talked about in front of my informant—Well, they fit patterns we recognize. Sorry I can’t be more forthcoming. You were one of a handful of candidates my organization singled out. You were one of the only ones to be found competent for this work.”*

*Gulls cried outside. It was midmorning and misty, but through the windows you could see white boats bobbing in the dark waters of Boston Harbor. Dawson’s office was on the twenty-ninth floor of the Custom House tower. The room was clean, bright, and had little furniture. You wondered if it was really Dawson’s office at all. The sole decoration was a photograph from his time with the 30*th *Division. It showed weary-looking men sitting expressionlessly in front of a huge black hole. That, Dawson had informed you, was the crucial Bellicourt Tunnel, an objective he and other Americans had helped the British and Australians capture in 1918.*

*“Will you be ready tomorrow?” he asked.*

*“Yes,” you said.*

ψ

*Several human heads, knit together by monstrous flesh into one being, scream and moan. One of them is Agent Dawson’s. His face presses against a membrane in the creature’s shoulder like a child’s face mashed against glass.*

flashback3.body:
Flashback III

*A path at the end of Church Street led to the ragged strip of beach where you’d agreed to meet Dawson. He was sitting on one of the big boulders that keep vigil on this part of the New England coast.*

*“Nice shell,” you said, observing the object he was studying.*

*“The prettiest thing I saw all day,” said Dawson.*

*“The grocery store is nice.”*

*“Well, it’s a chain… I have a question,” he said, handing you the shell. “Why does the town smell more like dead fish than the ocean?”*

*The shell was worn smooth. Curious marks on it looked like writing. You chucked it into the ocean.*

*“Because they catch the fish here and take them there,” you said. “Now I know why you wanted my help.”*

*Dawson didn’t laugh but stood up and brushed himself off. “From now on, we should stick together when we can. It looks depressing, but it* feels *dangerous. There’s absolutely no sign of her.”*

flashback4.body:
Flashback IV

*In some ways, the statue of the fishlike god wasn’t so different from a gaudy triton in a public fountain. But its proportions and embellishments were all wrong. The distance between the creature’s bulging eyes and its upper lip was short, and the mouth was three times that length and looked ready to swallow anything. The deity’s humanoid elements—arms, legs, hands—were long, unmuscled, and unfinished, but its robust tail and fins had intricate carvings and were polished to gleaming.*

*“Y’ha-nthlei,” chanted the voices down the hall over and over, rising and sinking in volume. A drum and brush accompanying them sounded like waves crashing. A flute or piccolo made gull-like shrieks. You hid behind the statue as two Innsmouth people shuffled down the corridor, through the shallow water, toward the harsh chorus. You followed.*

noResolution.body:
_If no resolution was reached because each investigator was defeated_: *Someone has found you and done their best to bring you back. In the darkness, you felt their hands and heard an underwater voice. As you regain consciousness you cough up brine. Seawater from your sinuses runs down your face. You are sitting, held gently up, gasping for air.*

*Then you see the sky and sun and moon. You could almost laugh for joy because you are alive on the surface of the world, but they forbid it: the sun is black, the pale moon sits beneath it, and the sky is dark red. The colors refract in the receding waves tugging at your clothes.*

*Your savior gasps your name. “Oh, thank goodness,” she says. “I really thought you were dead.”*

resolution1.body:
_Resolution 1_: *You emerge from the ocean tunnels and see that confusion afflicts the world, too. The sun is black, the pale moon sits beneath it, and the sky is dark red and glimmers on the rocky coast like blood. The sight is overwhelming, and despite your recent danger you want to sleep. You can’t, of course. You stand up.*

*Then, jarringly, someone yells your name.*

part1.body: *You know her voice. She speaks softly but deliberately. She has an Indian accent. You know her face, too, especially the deep-set, probing eyes.* T*his must be the woman you were with, the one you barely remembered when you woke up in the cave.*

aMeetingWithThomasDawson.body:
*“Elina,” you say.*

*“You say that like you’re not certain,” she says. “How are you doing?”*

*“I know we know each other, but I don’t remember much else.”*

*“Really? What about Dawson? Do you remember him?”*

*“Yes, barely. I think he’s—dead.”*

*“I thought you were both dead. Perhaps you’re wrong,” she says. The memory of Dawson encased in the monster’s flesh makes you shake your head.*

*“Dead, then,” she says. “What else? What happened?”*

*“I can’t tell you. I only remember pieces. I really don’t know what I’m doing here.”*

*“Hmm. The cure for amnesia can’t be sitting on a beach. Stand up. Move around a little bit. Perhaps the circulation will do your brain some good.”*

aBattleWithAHorrifyingDevil.body:
*You walk side- by-side. She seems to know where she is going, but she hasn’t told you. You know it isn’t home.*

*“What* do *you remember?*”

*“A ship called the* Grey Tern*. I saw the captain’s body in the caves.”*

*“The captain? He’s dead too? No wonder I couldn’t find him in town.”*

*“I remember being on his boat with him and fighting off a sea monster.”*

*“I suppose that’s from last week, when I was in Boston. You and Dawson went to Devil Reef…Two months ago, I would have laughed if anyone had told me something like that. Not now.”*

aDecisionToStickTogether.body:
*Elina scans the eastern horizon. You follow her gaze past a black, ridgelike formation in the water and start when you notice a ship almost out of sight. Two ships? Three?*

*“What are they doing here?” you ask.*

*“Who?” she asks.*

*You point.*

*“Goodness, I don’t know. The syzygy must have them confused too—but not as confused as you, I hope. Do you remember anything else?”*

*“Yes. Dawson sitting on the shore, saying we should stick together. He said Innsmouth was dangerous.”*

*“True. Obvious, but true. Good. Something more.”*

anEncounterWithASecretCult.body:
*“We are almost to Innsmouth,” Elina says. “We have a place to stay. The agency bought off the owner. I’ll explain everything there—Everything that’s happened since I saw you last, everything that happened before. Whatever you don’t know. I’ve been looking for you for the last three days.”*

*“There’s one other thing I remember,” you say. “A statue in a half-flooded basement. A chorus chanting* Y’ha-nthlei*.”*

*“The last message I had from Dawson was that you were going to investigate the Order of Dagon. That’s probably what you’re remembering.”*

*When you reach the tip of the cove you’ve been walking, you see a town on the next length of shoreline—tumbledown buildings, grand old houses from two centuries ago fallen into decrepitude, derelict boats, rotten docks. The stench of dead fish is oppressive. The few windows with glass look like red eyes in the weird light. South of you, across the cove behind you, you can now see the hazy beacon of a lighthouse.*[^1]

*“I know this place,” you say.*

*“You should. It’s Innsmouth,” Elina says. Her trench coat flaps around. Still wet, you shiver. “We now have a base on the very edge of town,” she says. “But we’ll still have to be as quick and quiet as we can.”*

intro1.body:
August 15, 1927

*“We’ve been up and down every street, but we haven’t seen her car. It’s time to start asking questions,” Dawson said as he parked in a dirt lot near Innsmouth’s abandoned railway station. You got out and began your search.*

*The townsfolk kept their distance. They seemed uniformly drab and ugly, and they shambled if they moved at all. Most were sedentary and kept to the shade; in fairness, it was a hot August afternoon. Though there was little grass to cushion their misshapen bodies, you saw several of them lying down. They exhibited a curious mix of human suspicion and animal indifference. Dawson attempted to draw them out, but they were so reticent that even the veteran agent’s determination began to flag.*
intro1.silasMarsh:
*It was just like you remembered, but somehow worse.*

*Offput by the town’s social character, you shifted your attention to its physical one. Excluding the coast, Innsmouth’s most remarkable natural feature was the river gorge of the Manuxet, which divided it in half and boasted two sets of wide and stupendous waterfalls. Between them was the town square. Mostly empty, you could imagine sailors, entertainers, merchants, and tramps passing through here in its more prosperous past.*

*At the square, Dawson told you he would explore the south part of town while you explored the north. He gave you a map and pointed out a strip of beach. “Follow Church Street. We’ll meet on the beach at 7 o’clock.”*

*There was a bus driver idling nearby and obviously eavesdropping. He drew back, surprised, when you walked up to him.*

*“Miss Harper?” he said in response to your question. “No Harpers around here.” Like many of the townspeople you’d seen, his eyes were large and glassy, and his face looked boneless.*

*“I don’t care if there are a hundred Harpers living here,” you said, “I’m looking for one named Elina, and I already told you she was a visitor.”*

*“Not a lot of visitors to Innsmouth.”*

*“I believe you.”*

*Eventually, your persistence paid off, and the driver—who said his name was Joe Sargent—told you a little about the town. But he evaded all questions about Harper in a very suspicious and unsatisfactory way.*

*Innsmouth proved unyielding. The more you pried, the worse it got, until it became clear that silent consensus had made you an object to be shunned. On Federal Street, a man walking toward you saw you and reversed course without turning around, shuffling backward on the sidewalk like a crab.*

*When you and Dawson met up, neither of you had any leads. “We’ll get rooms at the Gilman House,” he said, pointing to his map. “Elina told me she was staying there. We’ll try again tomorrow.”*

*You woke up early the next morning. No dreams.*

*“Someone’s done a good job of making it look like Elina was never here,” Dawson declared when you met up. “I examined the hotel’s books last night. There’s no entry for her. Nothing suspicious, either. It’s like she just vanished.”*

*With nothing more to go on than the agent’s conviction and Joe Sargent’s reluctantly given information, you continued the search. As it turned out, the second day of your investigation would be much more eventful than the first.*

This is a summary of the information conveyed to the investigators about the town of Innsmouth.

_First National Grocery_ Another person not originally from Innsmouth worked here. His name was Brian Burnham.

_The Gilman House_ An artist, Othera Gilman, was the proprietor of this shabby hotel.

_The Little Bookshop_ Sargent explained that Joyce Little owned this shop. He did not think highly of Joyce.

_The Marsh Refining Company_ Sargent spoke reverently of Barnabas Marsh, whose refinery was the town’s biggest industry.

_Fish Street Bridge_ A drunk named Zadok Allen loitered at this ruined bridge. Sargent called him a rascal and a liar.

_Innsmouth Harbour_ Sargent warned you to steer clear of the rough crowd at the harbor, and to take care to avoid a bully named Robert Friendly.

_New Church Green_ This area north of the square was the site of the Esoteric Order of Dagon, which Sargent described as a society “like the Masons.”

resolution1.body:
_Resolution 1_: *You couldn’t make it to your room. The stench made you dizzy, and the hostility wore you down. You found your way to the Manuxet and vomited into the dark waters.*

*Later that night, Dawson knocked on your door.*

*“I was checking up on you. Today was not an easy day.”*

*“I’m fine,” you lied.*

*“I’m not much better myself,” he said, ignoring the lie. He sat on a rickety chair by the window and looked out at the unlit town. The room was stifling and smelled like dead fish—just like every place in Innsmouth—and you’d opened the window hoping for a reprieve from the heat. You fancied you could hear the ocean.*

*“We’ve made ourselves too conspicuous. Another day like today and we’ll never find her or get to the bottom of what’s happening here. We need to study up. We should learn what we can about the Esoteric Order of Dagon, the society Elina was investigating before she disappeared. I don’t want to invoke the federal government quite yet, but we will if forced.”*

resolution2.body:
_Resolution 2_: *Brian Burnham had tied a burlap sack stamped with the First National name around Elina Harper’s head. You removed it and the gag she had in her mouth. The youth wept in the corner. “Don’t go anywhere,” you warned him.*

*Elina scrutinized you with wide eyes. “You’re here to free me, I hope,” she said. “Is Dawson with you?”*

*“He’s close by. How did this happen? This boy— Why did he do it?”*

*“He didn’t kidnap me, but he helped my kidnappers,” she said. “He was my jailor.”*

*“Listen, I’m a good Christian,” Burnham whined. “Last thing I wanted to do was hurt no one. But the Order told me they’d take away my job. You see, I saw them when they kidnapped her. They told me to shut up about it, and to keep me quiet they forced me to get involved. I had to do it, but I didn’t want to. They made me.”*

*He unbuttoned his shirt. His pale chest had several deep, ugly cuts in it.*

*“Did they do this to you?” you asked.*

*“I did it to me. But I wouldn’t have done it if—If I hadn’t—If they—"*

*“Tell us about them,” said Elina.*

resolution3.body:
_Resolution 3_: *“Oh Elina, Elina,” said Othera Gilman theatrically. She wasn’t fighting. She foamed at the mouth and wept despondently at the same time.*

*She’d led you to Elina Harper. Ropes bound the agent to a chair, and a flimsy Victorian screen painted with an unaccomplished seascape stood behind her. A canvas on an easel in front of the setup depicted a skinned woman tied to a ship’s mast.*

*“I’m sorry, Elina,” said Othera, “the dogs and cats want you back.”*[^2]

*As you freed Elina Harper, the agent scrutinized you with wide eyes. “Is Dawson with you?”*

*“He’s close by. How did this happen?”*

*“This woman drugged me, I think.”*

*Othera began to sing:*

*In Rome, the spritzer’s lemony, But Hydra has anemones— And if you’re not a perfect clown They’ll numb you up before you Drown. .*

*While she sang, you tied her up using Elina’s old bonds. She still didn’t resist.*

*“I don’t even know how long I’ve been here,” said Elina, rubbing her wrists and standing.*

*“Since I brought you here, silly,” said Othera.*

*Elina ignored her. “I’m looking forward to having rational conversations again,” she said. “But first we have to ask her some questions.”*

2
“In all these streets no living thing was visible, and I wondered at the complete absence of cats and dogs from Innsmouth” (*SOI*, p. 183).

resolution4.body:
_Resolution 4_: *“Miss Little,” you commanded. “Take me to Elina Harper.”*

*Joyce Little said nothing. She led you to a bolted and padlocked door and unlocked it. Beyond was a squalid, foul-smelling room. A tin of soup and a*

*plate of untouched crackers sat on the floor next to the chair where Elina Harper was tied up. Her eyes widened when she saw you. You began untying the ropes, watching Miss Little carefully the whole time.*

*When your work was done, Elina scrutinized you. “Is Dawson with you?”*

*“He’s close by. How did this happen?”*

*“This woman—” Elina began.*

*Joyce Little began to sob.*

*“I don’t understand why she kidnapped me,” Elina said. “She hasn’t said a word.”*

*“Miss Little,” you said sternly. “We need to ask you some questions.”*

*The woman grimaced and clutched her side. She groaned and bent over. You noticed a bulge where her rib cage was. Then a bloody fin broke through her shirt. On the opposite side, another fin popped out.*

*“I failed,” Miss Little said, groaning more. “They said if I couldn’t keep you safe this would happen. Oh my God, what is this?” Her hands were covered with blood and slime. The fins flapped slowly. “Why me?”*

*“Who? Who or what did this to you?” you asked.*

resolution5.body:
_Resolution 5_: *With his globe-like eyes, uncertain shape, and leprous skin, the reclusive owner of the Marsh Refinery was a perfect specimen of the “Innsmouth look.” When you bound his wrists behind his back you found that scaly skin sloughed off wherever you touched him. He spoke with a halting rasp. You wondered how he ran a business.*

*“Take me to her,” you demanded. He croaked something in response and led you to where Elina Harper was tied up and gagged.*

*“You must be with Dawson. Is he with you?” she asked after you freed her.*

*“He’s close by. How did this happen?”*

*“He’s been watching over me,” she said, indicating Barnabas, “but he didn’t kidnap me. It was a group of them. They came to the Gilman House one night, put a sack over my head, and brought me here.”*

*“You—shouldn’t have come to Innsmouth,” gurgled Barnabas to Elina. “But then I—told them—you should live. I bargained for you. I would have given you—this.” The man held out a long, unearthly necklace of silvery gold and fascinating, sea-green crystals as if presenting a gift. But then he shudderingly drew it back and began fondling it. “There is a place beneath the waters—it would have shown you,” he said, not making eye contact with either of them.*

*Painful-sounding coughs shook him. He dropped the necklace on the floor as if it meant nothing. Then he sat down in a chair, a sheen of sweat on his blubbery skin, and his legs started spasming violently. He jerked around so much that he nearly tipped his chair over, but he didn’t seem to notice.*

*“Tell us what’s going on here, Mr. Marsh,” said Elina.*

resolution6.body:
_Resolution 6_: *“I had to do it. They don’t want me talking, and I did talk. I talked to that fellow who looked at me the way Captain Obed did. They never gave me trouble afore because I took the first and second oaths of the Order,*[^3] *but Lord they were unhappy about that fellow who came in July and then with the government woman. They says to me, ‘*Listen here Zadok, you old drunk, you ain’t going to talk to anyone anymore at all if you don’t do as we says, and what we says is that you go to Gilman House with this bottle and clap that government woman on the head with it. After that you can have the bottle. Leave the woman for Pa Dagon and Mama Hydra.’ *And so I did as I was told, fer I was a poor wretch of a man and loved my life and my swill more than I loved some government lady foolish enough to nose about Innsmouth.”*

*“Take me to her,” you demanded.*

*He did. You found Elina Harper tied up and gagged.*

*“You must be with Dawson. Is he with you?” she asked after you freed her.*

*“He’s close by. Are you all right?”*

*“Yes. It was a light tap, all things considered. He was careful not to break the bottle.”*

*Zadok was contrite. “I’ll tell you everything I know, everything. I know what a sorry fool I’ve been. I don’t have much to live for now. I’m sure they’ll be a’coming for me soon. Might as well do something good afore the end.”*

3
Zadok tells the narrator of *SOI,* “They’d a kilt me long ago fer what I know, only I’d took the fust an’ secon’ Oaths o’ Dagon offen Obed, so was pertected unlessen a jury of ’em proved I told things knowin’ an’ delib’rit…but I wudn’t take the third Oath—I’d a died ruther’n take that—” (p. 197). Zadok Allen is, alas, the source of fifteen pages of tedious exposition in Lovecraft’s story. Additionally: “The government men never found poor Zadok, and have no conjectures to make as to what became of him” (*SOI*, p. 221). An inconsistency—or a coverup?

resolution7.body:
_Resolution 7_: *The sullen dockworker mumbled curses and insults incessantly as you questioned him, but he eventually gave up.*

*“I’ll take ’ee to ’er, just quit your prattling.”*

*At last, you found Agent Elina Harper tied up and gagged.*

*“You must be with Dawson. Is he with you?” she asked after you freed her.*

*“He’s close by. Are you all right?” you asked, noticing bruises on her face.*

*“Yes, no thanks to Mr. Friendly,” she said, indicating her kidnapper.*

*“You shoulda asked me to kill you,” he said. “Them marks aren’t nothing compared to what’s coming.”*

*“Tell us what’s coming,” demanded Harper, standing and rubbing her wrists.*

*“When you go in the water when the tide ain’t right—that’s what’s coming. When you think you can swim and can’t—That’s what’s coming. Do you know the tug of the undertow? That’s Father Dagon just breathing in. That’s all, just breathing in, bigger than human breath, bigger than the breath of a great whale-fish. And when you get tired and can’t go no more and give up, that’s Mother Hydra’s lullaby, that song we’re all gonna hear one day. And together they’re the end. What’s coming is the end. What’s coming is* their *city.”*

theSyzygy1.body:
_The Syzygy 1_: *Even as you watch the town of Innsmouth flood from the window of the flophouse, you relive those earlier scenes, conversations, and impressions. The waters rise; the memories return.*

*“You’re awake! What are you doing?! Come on,” says Elina Harper after she rushes into your room.*

theSyzygy2.body:
_The Syzygy 2_: *“My memory’s coming back. I don’t remember meeting you,” you say. “But I remember some of it. I remember looking for you with Dawson.”*

*“That’s good,” said Elina. “We met not long after. I escaped and found Dawson right where I expected him, at the Gilman House. You I did* not *expect. But enough reminiscence. Haven’t you seen? The sea is swallowing Innsmouth.”*

theSyzygy3.body:
_The Syzygy 3_: *“My memory’s coming back. I remember looking for you with Dawson. Rescuing you from your kidnapper,” you say.*

*“That’s wonderful,” she says. “But now is not the time for reminiscence. The sea is swallowing Innsmouth.”*

theSyzygy4.body:
_The Syzygy 4_: *You flee the building. The landlady is nowhere to be found, a fact Elina says she doesn’t like. Meanwhile, the sun and moon are rising in alignment, just like yesterday, and the water in the backyard is already deep. The skiff from the backyard is waiting for you. Elina had prepared it while you slept.*

*“If the waters are calm enough we can make the Annisquam River by noon. The town isn’t yet underwater, but at this rate I don’t give it long. Jump in.”*

intro.body:
*Elina is very handy with the skiff, and you are soon heading toward coastal waters. “The boat’s mine— or, more accurately, the agency’s. But this is my design,” she says, pointing out the scientific apparatus attached to the helm and hull.*

*“What’s it for?”*

*“You really do have amnesia. We’ve had this conversation at least three times. It helps me make maps of the ocean floor. Come on, use those oars. Or have you forgotten how to row, too?”*

*The waters are not calm, and the changing currents keep driving you back to the flooding, low-lying outskirts. You can still see the flophouse. “I knew I should have made the agency get me a motor,” Elina says. She advises you to use short, even strokes. You’re doing your best, but it’s getting harder and harder. She’s having trouble too.*

*“No! No!” she cries.*

*The boat is too heavy in the water.*

*“There’s a leak. How?” she asks. Neither of you says it, but you both think back to the landlady’s absence. “We need to find land, and fast.”*

*Luckily, the arduous journey has not taken you far, and the boat bears you to wadable terrain. “So much for my prototype,” Elina says when you are both out of the skiff. She opens the cylinder on the hull with a screwdriver and works to extract another cylindrical object set within. “What now?” she asks.*

*North and south of you, the shoreline is disappearing. You’re not far from the scattered rocks where you emerged yesterday.*

*“The only way seems to be through the town,” you say.*

*“You’re right. The highest ground is the old railway station, and the cars are there…Look! Over there! I don’t think we’ll meet many other refugees."*

*She points. Half-human, half-fish beings creep along the shore.*

*“You think they killed the townsfolk?”*

*“No. I think they* are *the townsfolk.”*

flashback5.body:
Flashback V

*Your excursion to Devil Reef shook your sense of reality. When Dawson asked, “There’s no* terra firma*, is there?” after the trip, you understood perfectly well that he didn’t just mean dry land.*

*Even so, land should have felt welcoming, but Innsmouth made you more uneasy than ever. You had become paranoid, always sure that someone was following you. The day before you broke into the Order of Dagon, you saw Joe Sargent’s bus idling in the town square. You accosted him.*

*“I see you watching me. Every time I come through here, you stare and stare. Why?” you demanded.*

*“Not much happening in Innsmouth. A bus driver has to look somewhere.”*

*“Oh yeah? How about I buy you a newspaper?” you said angrily.*

*Joe stared. Then he laughed. It was an unpleasant, croaking sound, but it was so strange, unexpected, and timely that you laughed too, despite yourself. “Look,” he said, “I don’t think you’re up to no good. I don’t trust you. And you and I both know you shouldn’t be here. So you can’t blame me if I look too much; I can’t help it. And I can’t read a word, so don’t buy me a paper. But I haven’t laughed in two years. I guess I owe you one.”*

In your Campaign Log, under “Memories Recovered,” record *a deal with Joe Sargent.*

Put the set-aside Joe Sargent asset into play under the control of an investigator at Innsmouth Square.

flashback6.intro:
*“What’s back here?” Dawson whispered.*

*“*The Life of George Washington *in five volumes.”*

*“John Marshall’s biography? I read that at West Point. I know this one too,” he said, pointing with his flashlight. “The* Bay Psalm Book. *First book printed in America. This is a reprint, of course.” He handed you the light and opened to a random page:*

*With thy plenteous store the earth is fully frought. So is this great & spatious _sea_ wherein things creepeth.*
flashback6.believer:
*“Psalm 104,” you said, recognizing the verse.*

*He flipped the page and read. “So it is. Good memory.”*
flashback6.otherwise:
*“I hope no sea thing creepeth in Miss Little’s bookstore,” you said.*

*“We creepeth ourselves,” ventured Dawson.*

*“We creep. I don’t think we creepeth.”*

*The bookstore had been closed since Elina came back. Now she was in Boston, using the Submarine Signal Company’s facilities for some of the opaque scientific research she was doing for the government. You had all agreed that you needed more information about the Order of Dagon and Devil Reef, and the one place with books in town—there were no libraries—was the shop. It was 2 in the morning. You’d broken in, and you hadn’t discovered anything, not even in the secretive- looking alcove you were now investigating. Idly, you pulled out one of the volumes of the Washington biography.*

*Another book sat behind it, perpendicular, flat against the wall, its binding sea-black.*

*Scraping. A knock. A noise at the front of the shop. Dawson shut off the flashlight.*

*“They’ve found us,” he hissed. “Back door. Run.”*

ψ

*The mysterious book is still in the alcove, but you feel Dawson’s absence.*

flashback7.body:
Flashback VII

*Agents Harper and Dawson did not always work well together. Dawson’s reserve, dry humor, and supreme trust in two authorities—the U.S. government and his soldier’s intuition— distinguished him from Elina, a cosmopolitan, scientific-minded pragmatist happy enough to work for Uncle Sam while he funded her research. They differed on everything, inauspicious for an operation whose success depended on unanimity and understanding. One night, they’d quarreled.*

*It was a week before Devil Reef. At that point, the three of you were staying at a motel near Ipswich: you’d decided to leave town after Dawson observed regular spies posted in the alley adjacent to the Gilman House. You overheard the quarrel through the thin walls between your room and Dawson’s.*

*“I don’t understand why you think there’s a deadline,” Elina was saying. “In two weeks, it’ll be ready. Then we use it to complete the map of Devil Reef.”*

*“No. We can’t wait two weeks. It’s my gut— Something is* happening *in Innsmouth.”*

*“That’s very evident to me. I was kidnapped. But how can your gut tell the difference between one and two weeks? Let me tell you: this is the more prudent way. Knowing the terrain will make it safer.”*

*“You don’t care about safety. You just want to test your new equipment.”*

*Elina lowered her voice then. You could still hear her, but you couldn’t make out the words. When Dawson responded, he matched her volume. The two went back and forth like that until, finally, you knocked on the door.*

*“I overheard you arguing,” you said when Dawson let you in. “I don’t understand why I wasn’t included in the discussion, but I agree with Dawson. I’ve been having the dreams again. A voice is calling from Devil Reef. We need to go there.”*

In your Campaign Log, under “Memories Recovered,” record *an intervention.*

flashback8.intro:
*Dawson knew the local police could not be trusted, but he also took the rule of law seriously. The kidnapper’s guilt was obvious, but the usual legal proceedings—not, as Elina insisted, an immediate, thorough interrogation at the agency’s Boston offices—would have to be observed. In the meantime, the culprit would stay in the Innsmouth jail, and you would visit daily. (“Good for you,” Elina remarked. “I’ll abstain. I’ve done* my *time.”) With any luck, you’d be able to extract some concrete information.*

*After three mornings of visits, you doubted you’d get anything at all.*
flashback8.brianBurnham:
*Brian had changed his tune. He said he had orchestrated the whole thing, that he was erotically fascinated by Elina Harper, that he had long struggled with his hateful lust and carved those marks into his flesh out of self-punishment. When you reported this to Elina, she laughed. “Were those his actual words?! ‘Erotically fascinated’? My oh my.”*

*Mr. Burnham stuck to this story. Dawson was impressed by how uncrackable the young man could be.*
flashback8.otheraGilman: *Othera’s madness seemed to have had some method in it when you apprehended her; now, she was pure Ophelia. She danced around the room, tried biting through the bars, would act sane and ready to answer questions and then give you a recipe for marmalade or bash her head against the walls until she bled.*
flashback8.joyceLittle: *You had witnessed Joyce’s horrific transformation, but every time you brought it up, she looked at you strangely and denied it. She wore concealing clothes, and when you commented on her pallor and raspy voice, she said she was ill. “Probably because this cell is so damp,” she said. “I miss my store. I don’t know why you’re asking me all these questions; like I said, I don’t remember anything.”*
flashback8.barnabasMarsh:
*Mr. Marsh’s lawyer, a Boston Brahmin without any trace of the Innsmouth look, was always there and spoke in his client’s stead. Dawson was a smart agent, but playacting was not his strong suit, and on the last morning, the lawyer put* him *on the defensive.*

*“You said you were with the Federal Trade Commission and wanted to question Mr. Marsh privately about the refinery’s gold production. I took that very seriously. Well, Mr. Phillips,” he said, emphasizing the alias, “my firm has a stack of* Washington Evening Stars *going back fifty years. I had one of my paralegals look for the public notice of your appointment. She didn’t find any. Who are you really, Mr. Phillips?”*
flashback8.zadokAllen:
*Zadok’s cell always reeked of alcohol, and its inmate was always in a stupor. Dawson asked the jailor how he was getting spirits, but the jailor denied that he’d had any. “Old Zadok’s lived a life of drinking and storytelling, and now things have taken a hard turn. He’s in shock is all.”*

*On the third day, the smell of spirits was fainter and Zadok was more lucid. Despite these good omens, the most you could get from him was: “They got me. They finally did. The change is coming.”*
flashback8.robertFriendly:
*“Father Dagon sits in a chamber underwater. He’s full of lies as good as truths. Mother Hydra sleeps and dreams truths as bad as lies. Between them, they got us covered. The ocean’s got us covered. Now water can’t be held. Now water can’t be breathed. Now water can’t be a window where you see the sun. But even so that’s where the city is, the rising city, the city that’ll make Boston and New York and all the rest look like blocks that babies throw around. You can see it. Look hard. Look inside.”*

*This and other talk like it were all you could get out of Robert Friendly, no matter what tack Dawson took.*

*On the fourth day, the jail cell was empty.*

*“What happened here?!” asked Dawson.*

*“It’s very embarrassing, sir,” said the warden, not embarrassed at all. “I don’t know. I must have dozed off. When I woke up, there was the prison— but no prisoner.”*

*Dawson tried indignant bluster and reprimands, but the warden just shook his head and shrugged. He seemed to feel sorry for you.*

noResolution.body:
_If no resolution was reached because each investigator was defeated_: *You’re sure you’re drowning. It’s preferable to the confusion of almost drowning. Will it be painful? Will you be afraid? Yes and yes. It is painful. You are afraid. You panic, and your head breaks the water. Is that you bellowing like an animal? Yes. You will cling to life after all, you have to.*

*“Oh my God! I thought you were gone!” cries Elina. She puts her arm around you, steadying you against the current as you splutter and cough. “Again, you cheat death—Well, for an hour maybe.”*

*You are chest-deep in the floodwaters. “Where are we?”*

*“West of the town square and not far from the station. But those fish people are everywhere, and the river wants us to go where it’s going.”*

*Half-swimming, half-walking, and at one point hiding behind debris eddying waters had gathered in an intersection, you finally make it to the railway station.*

resolution1.body:
_Resolution 1_: *You find the agents’ vehicles parked in the station’s dirt lot. Expecting slashed tires and broken windows, you find instead two state-of-the-art vehicles in almost pristine condition, gleaming in the fading, ruddy light.*

*“Get in. Let’s go,” said Elina. “I’m sorry we’ll have to leave Dawson’s car behind.”*

*You reach into your pocket reflexively and pull out a car key; you realize you have had it this whole time but just now understood what it was.*

*“You are full of surprises,” Elina said. “Good. We* can *take both. Unless…Hmm. Maybe traveling together would be safer. I just don’t know.”*

*“But* where *are we going?” you ask.*

*“Ipswich, then Boston. We need to tell the agency about Dawson and everything else. Then we come back with a larger team.”*

*“Come back for what? Do we even have that long?” you ask.*

*She considers this and finally shakes her head. “Wake up, Elina,” she says to herself. “You’re right. We* don’t *have that long. This isn’t normal. We can’t be sure about anything anymore. I was wrong. I should have listened before and gone with you to Devil Reef.”*

*That name again. Devil Reef. You see it, jagged and forbidding. White spray against black rocks. Seabirds wheeling around above you, warning you away. Devil Reef. You remember it.*

intro1.body:
September 2, 1927

*The* Grey Tern*’s captain wasn’t a local. Beaufort Moore fished the waters between Prince Edward Island and Boston and had discovered the bounty of bluefish, bass, and cod near Innsmouth. Others had discovered this, too, but the town’s hostility kept them away. In all of Captain Moore’s long life, however, no one had ever succeeded in discouraging him. He liked everybody, trusted they liked him back, and was oblivious to all surly suggestions that he’d “better look for other spots.” His good humor wore out the townsfolk, and they put up with him.*

*“Of course, that’s not what* he *says,” Dawson told you. “But that’s the situation. He’ll take us. I told him we were with a concrete company out of New York and paid him very well.”*

*Once again missing Harper—she was in Boston— you and Dawson boarded the trawler on an overcast Friday morning. “Are you sure you wouldn’t rather go to Plum Island?” Captain Moore asked. “It’s a safer place than that ugly ridge. I won’t tell if you won’t.”*

*“Unfortunately, no,” said Dawson. “We need to collect samples from the reef. If anything happens to the boat, our company will compensate you.”*

intro2.body:
_Intro 2_: *Your interviews with Elina Harper’s kidnapper had yielded little coherent information.*

*Still, the evidence suggested the Esoteric Order of Dagon was behind that and other misdeeds, including the doings reported by the witness who’d fled Innsmouth in July. Attempts to talk to members of the Order were rebuffed, but Dawson said it wasn’t yet time to invoke the authority of the federal government. “We’re on strict orders not to make a scene,” he’d said. “They know we’re with the government, but that’s about it.”*

*For the time being, then, the Esoteric Order of Dagon was a closed door. But Devil Reef—Devil Reef also featured in the story of what happened in July. According to the witness, the Order’s practices and the formation were connected.*

*Now you approached the ill-famed ridge. From afar, you had imagined jutting rocks like what you’d seen on the coast. But these were immense—islands and islets, really, not rocks. The seabirds that ought to have haunted them kept their distance, screaming and circling above.*

*“This isn’t going to be smooth,” said Moore. “There’s a reason I only took my boat here once. The shoals shift, the currents shift too. I don’t believe what people say about the reef—I don’t scare easily. But my boat does.”*

flashback9.body:
Flashback IX

*You found a statuette made of heavy, platinum-like material. It looked abstract at first, just a design given three dimensions, but studying it convinced you its maker wanted to capture the likeness of something—the likeness of something* unlike *anything you knew.*

*Spines covering the thing’s arms or tentacles bent slightly when you touched them. They sprang back when you removed your fingertips, as if organic. Dominating the work was a sea-green crystal set in its center. Eye? Orifice? Some alien organ? When you stared into it you lost yourself in its depths, depths that seemed to begin near an inner shore— sank into a green abyss—and ended in black, eternal, starless space.*

flashback10.body:
Flashback X

*The ruins beneath Devil Reef filled you with awe and uncertainty. Their grandeur was unlike that of the Pyramids or the Roman Forum or the temple cities of Mesoamerica. The architecture was on a different scale, built by hands that could not have been human. It trivialized the world you knew, its history, and its peoples. Conflicts over national boundaries and cultural differences were nothing, human art nothing, music just a cry in a wilderness of nothing. When you reached an object that might have been an altar, you had to stop yourself from kneeling before it.*

*Beside the altar stood a statue with human proportions. It looked unfinished. Roughly chiseled, it had no distinguishing features except its height and build, which were the same as yours. Draped over its shoulders was a cloak with aquamarine beadwork and embroidered with gold thread. It looked like satin but felt like skin. You took it; it fit you. Later, you would wonder why.*

flashback11.body:
Flashback XI

*You entered a cavern where two statues stood, one of black onyx, one of white marble. They forbade thought, demanded wonder, and compelled you forward. You strode through a half-circle of people you recognized from Innsmouth and, strange to say, other people from your more distant past—from before Innsmouth, from your old life, even from childhood. You were invisible to them, you realized. When you should have brushed against someone, you walked through them.*

*“This is the Temple of the Union,” intoned a priestess in silver and green dress. Silver fins ran up and down her arms, and her eyes continually bled silver. Loops of pearl and sea-green crystals hung over her breasts, and on her head was a platinum crown or coronet. She had two fishtails, one predominantly black, one predominantly white, both mottled with the opposite color. “Reconcile with us. You have heard Mother’s call.”*

*You knew you had mere moments. You were drowning—not in water, but in the inhospitable ether of a reality hostile to yours. She reached out to you, but you slapped her hand away, and she recoiled. The coronet fell from her head, and you seized it. She and the semicircle of phantoms vanished. You ran from the temple holding the strange headdress.*

resolution1.body:
_Resolution 1_: *No one spoke on the way back to Innsmouth. The adventure had rattled Captain Moore, and for the first time in his life he was pensive. You felt guilty: it was clear your business at Devil Reef had nothing to do with collecting samples for a concrete company, but the man was too good-natured to say anything about it. You watched as the ridge grew smaller, almost worried it and its secrets would come striding after you. Beyond the ridge, at the horizon, you thought you saw several shadows, black blocks sitting on the cusp of sea and sky.*

*Back in Innsmouth, you confronted Dawson.*

*“Those things—those places—those creatures. You knew.”*

*“Knew?” he asked, surprised. “I told you about the report we had in July. I had no idea the witness wasn’t exaggerating—that if anything he was downplaying his experiences.”*

*“Dawson, tell me what the government’s doing here.”*

*“We are investigating paranormal activity in Innsmouth and its surroundings.”*

*“Yes. But what else? What* is *the agency I’m risking my life for? What is its ultimate mission?”*

*Dawson looked distressed. “When Elina gets back—We’ll talk about it then.”*

*“If we were back in Ipswich, I’d leave. I’d take the train back to Arkham or Boston.”*

*“Don’t say that. You’ve been invaluable to us, to me,” Dawson said earnestly. “What I mean is— you’ve kept me—sane. I mean it. Just wait. You’ll know everything. You have my word.”*

*It was night. The town was dark, as always, except for the light of the lighthouse at Falcon Point. You watched the beam’s slow rotation illuminating nothing and everything in the circle it traced.*

beneathTheWaves1.body:
*“Devil Reef! The lighthouse!” you exclaim to Elina. She’s opening the car door in the train station’s dirt lot. “They were angry at us for trespassing in Devil Reef. They took us to the lighthouse.”*

*“Your memories are coming back?”*

*“Yes!”*

*“What’s this about the lighthouse?”*

*“I think that’s how I ended up in the caves.”*

*“I don’t see the connection of these ideas,” she says, closing the car door partway.*

*“I don’t either,” you admit. “But I’m certain: I was at the lighthouse with Dawson. Members of the Order of Dagon brought me there. That was before the caves.”*

*“Oceiros Marsh is the lighthouse keeper,” says Elina. “Like almost everyone in town, he belongs to the Order of Dagon. He’s high up, I think.”*

*You recognize the name instantly. “Yes. He’s the one responsible. He’s behind it all.”*

*“Then we go to the lighthouse and confront him. We have no other options. You can drive. Do you remember anything else?”*

interlude3.purpleKey:
*“Sea-green crystal?” she asks when you describe the idol you found. “How large?”*

*“Smaller than my fist, but not by much.”*

*“Ah. Wonderful! Was it pleochroic?”*

*“Excuse me?”*

*“Mmm—Nothing. I wonder what happened to it. The cultists must have seized it.”*
interlude3.whiteKey:
*“Who would have thought?” you ponder. “Those alien-seeming ruins here, right off the coast of Massachusetts? How did they come to be here?”*

*“I don’t know,” says Elina. “I haven’t seen them myself—not exactly—but we do know about the existence of several extensive subaquatic structures.”*

*“‘Extensive’? Infinite,” you say. You talk about the altar, the unfinished statue, and the cloak you took.*

*“A cloak? How odd. Sounds ugly, too. Why did you take it?”*

*“I’m not sure. The material was strange. It didn’t get wet.”*

*“*That *would have been useful earlier. I’m still soaked.”*
interlude3.blackKey:
*Harper looks at you with concerned scrutiny when you bring up your surreal encounter with the priestess.*

*“Was that a hallucination linked to your amnesia, or did something like that truly happen?”*

*“It didn’t feel real even then. But the headdress I took was real—I’m certain of that.”*

*“There’s a similar object back in Boston. The government has it on permanent loan from the Newburyport Historical Society. It was in their collection for years, despite repeated offers from the Marsh family to reacquire it.*[^4] *The witness from earlier in the summer told us about it.”*

*“What do you think of it?” you ask.*

*“It’s a fantastic thing. No human made it, but that’s probably obvious—At this point, I believe we can take for granted that non-human, intelligent life is a reality. As for the ‘tiara,’ as we call it…It’s been extremely important for my research. Crucial, even. I—”*

4
See *SOI*, pp. 166-168.
interlude3.noKeys: *You talk about your adventures at Devil Reef as images of the day come to you— the mask-like cheer of Captain Moore as he ferried you from one islet to another; the serf-filled caverns and glimpses of subaquatic structures; glassy, ravenous eyes… But, you think self-consciously, gaps in the narrative are making it rambling and unbelievable. Elina is doing her best to follow.*
interlude3.beneathTheWaves2:
*A blaring car horn interrupts the conversation. You check the rearview mirror.*

*“Who’s that?” she wonders, turning around in her seat. You slow down. It’s dusk, and the coastal country road is already dark. All you can see are headlights. They’re getting closer.*

*“Don’t slow down,” she says.*

*“From Innsmouth, you think?” you ask.*

*“Yes. Go fast. Faster.”*

*“We’re going to the lighthouse still, yes?”*

*“Yes. I know the way. Fast!”*

intro.body:
*Your pursuer is closing on you. They are driving recklessly. You are driving recklessly, too. You have to. You have no sense of anything but the road, your car’s headlights, and the darkness all around.*

*There are mysteries. What you’re doing here, what Elina is after, what those people, or half-people, or monsters behind you want. Where your memories went and why they went there. But right now, mysteries don’t matter. What matters is speed.*

_Resolution 1_: *The worst of the harrowing drive is past. At Elina’s insistence, you pull into a turnaround near the base of the crag where the lighthouse stands.*

*“Drive into the woods,” said Elina.*

*“There’s no road!”*

*“I know. Drive in as far as you can. We don’t want anyone seeing the car. We’ll continue on foot.”*

*When you can drive no further, you get out and start walking. As you go, you keep the road to Falcon Point in sight, fearing to see more cars drive up to the lighthouse and cut you off. But the road remains empty.*

*Through the trees, you can just make out the dusky Atlantic. Fragments of sky turn blood-red while a scarlet sun rises.*

*“Sailors take warning,” says Elina.*

intro.body:
*The lighthouse sits at the easternmost tip of a promontory jutting into the ocean. From somewhere, you recall that the name Falcon Point comes from how the cliffs on either side of it look when drawn on a map. They curve symmetrically, like wings, with the promontory the bird’s head. There’s even a hooklike pile of jagged rocks south of the lighthouse suggesting a falcon’s beak.*

*When you emerge from the woods, sunrise is complete, and the glimmering pinks, roses, reds, and crimsons of the ocean and sky hold you and Elina spellbound. A band of dense fog sits beneath the heavens, over the sea, its roof alive with reflected colors.*

*“We should go,” says Elina. She tugs at you.*

*But you can’t go, not yet. The sea’s beacon and the world’s stare at each other across the foggy ocean. You have the strong, absurd idea that they are in communion, speaking to each other in a language of light and omens. Then fog and clouds drift before the sun, and morning gloom swallows the sunrise.*

flashback12.body:
Flashback XII

*On the way to Devil Reef, Captain Moore pointed out the lighthouse. “It’s a shame—There wouldn’t be a handsomer lighthouse on the Atlantic if the Marshes kept it up. Still, it’s regular as can be, save for twice a year, when it goes dark. I once asked a local about the rumor that there was a nest of caves beneath it, and he said there was and that he’d seen ’em himself. Then he told me the biggest lie I’ve ever heard.”*

*“What was that?” you asked.*

*“‘When Obed Marsh ordered the lighthouse built,’ he says to me, ‘there was already caves there. But Obed said that wasn’t gonna be enough. No one knew what he meant, but he had so many caves dug out you could walk clear from the top of the lighthouse to the bottom of the ocean. Eventually, Obed said, he’d show everyone why he needed them. And so, one day, he opened the grates and gates and doors that kept the sea out. The tide came in; the tide went out. Then he called everyone to the lighthouse to look at what the sea left behind.’*

*‘Every cell, every cranny, ceiling to floor, floor to ceiling, was filled with fish. Every kind, from every part of the world. And he said the lighthouse was a great big lure and that someday he’d catch the biggest fish of all.’”*

*Captain Moore laughed and laughed at the memory. “These Innsmouth folks!”*

flashback13.body:
Flashback XIII

*Before you ever came to Innsmouth, you had a recurring dream about the town. You had it when you stayed at the motel in Ipswich, too. You never had the dream in Innsmouth itself. It varied, but the fundamentals were always the same. This was the dream:*

*For long days you have wandered the salt marshes south of Innsmouth. You are growing. You are trying to get to the town. The fierce birds hate you, and so do the hair-covered animals. Even the fish only stare at you before they jerk away. You loathe the wan green of salt hay grass and the harsh glow of goldenrod. You want the baleful sun bleeding and dead. You should not be here: She is calling in the deeps.*

*Later, you are bigger. Your body seethes with hateful appetites, your mind with hateful questions. Why are you here? Why must you roam in this wilderness of simple flesh? What is Mother and Father’s plan? The town is no closer; you are still trying to get to it. It is urgent. You should not be here: She is calling in the deeps.*

*You dream of being eldest, of floating over abysses where only mind can swim. You dream of gliding through the port beneath the sea, over sapphire- black voids, in chasms carved by fear, through arches that have known only starlight. You dream of staring through sea-green asymmetries at the loathsome, bone-dry, sunlit world you inhabit, and saying, “Now I am home.”*

In your Campaign Log, under “Memories Recovered,” record *the lifecycle of a “Deep One.”*

_Resolution 1_: *The dreadful cat-and-mouse game in the lighthouse ends where everything began, on the rocks of the Atlantic. You and Elina sit there in silence, reflecting on what you’ve seen, looking out over the expanse of black sea and red sky.*

*“How are you?” she asks, just when you’re about to speak. She’s sitting on a boulder with her feet dangling above the breakers. She pulls her legs up onto the rock as if suddenly aware how much she resembles a beachgoer.*

*“I remember more,” you say, mulling over new scenes you see playing in your mind’s eye. The lighthouse—its denizens, its caves, its stench—has triggered more memories. They come from the past, one after the other, overwhelming the present—The Order of Dagon. Capture. Dawson. You watch as waves hit the shore.*

*“A few more scrapes with death, and you’ll remember everything. I joke, of course. It’s good your memory is coming back,” she says.*

*“Is it?” you ask. The waves keep coming.*

resolution3.body:
_Resolution 3_: *You see a light, but is it below you or above? You swim toward it, then toward darkness, then toward light, then toward anything—you are twisting in the water. A fire burns your aching lungs. This is how it ends? This? Of course it is.*

*You are among the first victims of the deluge. The waters rise inch by inch at first, then foot by foot, then tower by tower, on the last day covering the tip of Sagarmatha, and then drowning even the memory of land. Hordes attack the vessels with which some people seek to save themselves. A thousand desperate armadas sink to the ocean floor. The skies are filled with frantic birds for several weeks. Then they empty of life, and starlight and moonlight and sunlight pour down on a world where nothing breathes.*

*And still the waters rise. The springs are infinite. Hydra and Dagon dip their ladles in the ever- flowing fountain of brine and ooze. They are the cupbearers of all the Old Ones, and they wait for the exiles to come to repossess the reality that was and is to be theirs, sailing in on their great ships. Unhearable choruses sing the name Cthulhu. The stars shudder.*

*G*LORY TO *D*AGON*! G*LORY TO *H*YDRA*! G*LORY TO *Y’*HA*-*NTHLEI*,* PORT OF THE *O*LD *O*NES*! I*T IS YOUR TIME*.*

intro1.body:
September 5, 1927

*It was late summer, almost midnight. The town was as quiet as always. A sea breeze, mild and salty, had granted Innsmouth a reprieve from its fishy miasma. Neither warm nor cool, the air was so humid that the breeze felt like a caress.*

*“Did anyone follow us?” Dawson whispered.*

*“Yes.”*

*Dawson looked back. “Gone?”*

*“A block ago,” you said.*

*“It was clear where we were going.”*

*“It’s the only place anyone goes at night.”*

*You had taken Federal Street from the town square. A single incandescent streetlamp lit the area. In its dim halo, the sedge of New Church Green looked wild, and the park’s two dilapidated churches looked forlorn and haunted. Your destination, the headquarters of the Order of Dagon, was similarly shabby—but it vibrated and thrummed with an energy, a music, a voice, which told a very different story.*

*“What is that?” you asked.*

*“What?” asked Dawson.*

*“The building, that sound—If it is a sound.”*

*“I don’t hear anything,” he said.*

*You listened again. “I know it from the dreams. This is close to where it comes from.”*

*Dawson looked pensive. Your psychic sensitivity to what was happening in Innsmouth hadn’t provided any real information, despite dutiful record-keeping and long interviews with both agents. Your dreams had enhanced rather than shed light on mysteries, and Agent Harper frankly suspected they were simply tricks your enemies used to manipulate the investigation. Most recently, they had led you to Devil Reef—an adventure with decidedly mixed results.*

*But Dawson was thinking about something else. “Last night—” he began.*

*“Another time,” you said.*

*He looked relieved.*

intro2.body:
_Intro 2_: *He looked up at the portico and looming door. “Do you think it’s true? What Elina’s kidnapper said about Dagon that last time?”*

*“That he sleeps beneath Devil Reef? That he sleeps beneath us, wherever we are?” you asked.*

*“Yes. Do you think it’s true? Do you think Dagon is real?”*

*“Yes, but not like us. Not the way we are.”*

intro3.body:
_Intro 3_: *“Do you think it’s true?” Dawson asked. “The dream you had about Dagon?”*

*You shuddered. “It was not a dream.”*

*“Sorry. Nightmare, then. You said you were certain you’d seen him—that he was real, and that you’d seen him. Do you still believe that?”*

*“Yes. I think he’s real. But not the way we are. Not like us.”*

_Intro 4_: *“I hope you’re wrong. I hope he’s not,” said Dawson. Then he handed you a key. “For the car. It’s a copy, in case you make it out and I don’t. Let’s go.” With that, he opened the door.*

*If you had screamed you couldn’t have made more noise. The door creaked like a tree limb ready to fall. You entered a surprisingly grand hall. Though it was dim, you could easily make out a double staircase and, inlaid in the center of the marble floor, the All-Seeing Eye of the Masons.*

*“Here we are,” said Dawson. “Stay close.”*

noResolution.body:
_If no resolution was reached (each investigator resigned or was defeated)_: *The grand entryway was quiet. Dust lay over everything in the hall, undisturbed for years. The door had fallen in, but nobody had thought to come repair it.*

*Then the All-Seeing Eye inlaid in marble on the floor twitched, and you came rushing back through. You pulled open the door and jumped down the steps into horror.*

*There was a crowd there. Who were these people? They threw themselves upon you. You twisted and wriggled, but one had your ankle in her wet hands. You slipped from the grasp, but your effort propelled you into the arms of a squelching, sighing man with rank breath. They were disconcertingly noiseless; they stared and gaped and thrashed about without much sound. Their clumsiness didn’t matter because there were so many. You had to give up. Faint and nauseous, you collapsed. You vomited as they kicked you. Some of them flopped down on the ground beside you, spent.*

resolution1.body:
_Resolution 1_: *You had no idea what was going on. You couldn’t remember anything. You were gagged. The man someone kept calling “the government man” was lying nearby in a fetal position. They had taken you to a lighthouse. Your captor said he was the lighthouse keeper and called himself Oceiros.*

*Other people were bound here, too. Most of them were unconscious.*

*The lighthouse keeper knelt beside the government man. He had a house painting brush and was using it to apply a slimy substance to his body. The other captives had been given the same treatment, but not you. Not yet. As Oceiros worked, he rambled. Occasionally, the government man wriggled in his bonds.*

*“Grandpa Obed was a vicious man. Earth-sighted. When he brought Dagon’s creed he didn’t know what he was doing. He thought he’d make deals with Father Dagon the way the witches did when they called up whoever and asked for buried treasure. ‘Oh spirit, tell me where the buried treasure is…’ You’re not so different from that, government man. You want to say to Dagon, ‘Oh spirit, tell me where the buried treasure is.’ Sick. Barbarians always ransack the temple before they raze the city. Sick. So much beauty lost.”*

*You groaned involuntarily.*

*“The dreamer’s up,” said Oceiros quietly, looking your way. He’d ripped the government man’s shirt and was painting his torso. “The dreamer’s seen some of it, government man. Inhuman beauty, nemesis beauty, it hates sordid puking human life and squares with square corners. It hates things with fur and things as they are. Earth-sighted beauty is all a little ramshackle. Down in the abyss is the real stuff that goes all the way to the stars.*

*Obed didn’t see that. He didn’t know the beauty of the Old Ones, serene and fleshless. I’ve seen it, though: But I can’t know it. Only THEY know it. They have it, their beauty. Their beauty is their right to the world. We don’t have their beauty and we don’t have their right. Look at Innsmouth. Look at you, government man. Look at me. We’re wrong, all wrong. But we can serve; we can be their subjects and make way for them. Do you want to be their herald, government man? They are many and need a herald with many heads, many hands.”*

*As he talked, you realized the ropes around your wrist were slippery enough to manipulate. You groaned again, this time to interrupt. You needed to do something.*

*“What is it, dreamer? You have something to say?” Oceiros asked. He laid the brush on the government man’s chest and then ungagged you.*

resolution2.body:
_Resolution 2_: *Your hands freed, you punched Oceiros as he leaned over you, sending him reeling. You leapt to your feet and sprang to the government man. But Oceiros was completely unharmed, and before you could even think of untying your fellow prisoner, he was on top of you and hit you with a backhand.*

*“That was nasty of you,” the lighthouse keeper said after he tied you up again. “You aren’t fit for this. To the tides with you.”*

*Oceiros opened a metal hatch in the chamber floor. The government man watched, his eyes wide with pain and grief, as the lighthouse keeper pushed you into the hole. You fell into the cave and hit your head on the rock.*

ψ

*The government man sat in front of the pool of black water where your memory went. He was writing on a seashell. He looked up, expressionless, and shook his head. “Wake up soon,” he said. “Remember me.”*

*“Guppy, guppy,” he chided as he tied you up again. “Back in your net. Then to the tides with you.”*

_Resolution 4_: *“Please don’t hurt us,” you said. “I’ve lost my memory. I don’t know what we’re doing here. I don’t mean you any harm.”*

*“Forget all your dreams, dreamer? That’s too bad. Let me help you remember. You and the government people came to Innsmouth because of what that man saw in July—Trust a descendant of Obed Marsh to muck things up. You all think Innsmouth is strange and lawless and that the people smell bad. You suspect we make sacrifices on Devil Reef. You think we’ve gone far enough. You want to destroy Y’ha-nthlei. But first you want to rob it. So, dreamer, I don’t care what you have to say. I’m a little too good for your pleas and your bad reasoning. Tell it to the tides.”*

*Oceiros opened a metal hatch in the chamber floor. The government man watched, his eyes wide with pain and grief, as the lighthouse keeper pushed you into the hole. You fell into the cave and hit your head on the rock.*

hiddenTruths.intro:
*“That was the last you saw him, then?” Elina asks.*

*“Yes. The last time I saw him as he was.”*

*“I’m sorry,” she says.*

*“*I’m *sorry,” you say. “You knew him longer than I did.”*

*“It’s strange you’d already lost your memory. I assumed the cause was head trauma you suffered in the caves.”*

ψ

*You were sailing again. You had no choice. The water had risen all day. You had found an abandoned boat not far from the lighthouse. You had debated where to go, but the sea did not care about your debate. It pushed you north, toward Devil Reef. You had little strength to fight the current. You knew you were sailing into doom, but the setting sun and moon reminded you that doom was inescapable no matter where you went.*

*“I need to know, Elina,” you say. “Not that it matters now. But—Why* are *we here? Dawson said he was going to tell me.”*

*“Of course. We have a moment. You know what I study, yes?”*

*“Oceanography,” you say.*

*“Sonar technology specifically. Mapping the ocean floor and detecting objects in the water. Useful for many things—subaquatic construction, shipping, submarines.”*

*“How does it work?”*

*“A signal is sent into the ocean; an echo of the signal comes back, and that echo tells the scientist something about what’s there. Quartz crystal is piezoelectric, which means it is capable of sending and receiving this signal. It is useful and abundant, but the band of frequencies it can transmit is limited.”*
hiddenTruths.science: “Ah yes. I broadly understood the concept, but I couldn’t remember the mechanism. But what does this have to do with Innsmouth?”
hiddenTruths.otherwise:
“What does this have to do with Innsmouth?”

*“When the agency turned up artifacts from the town made of unknown materials, they analyzed the crystals and discovered that they were piezoelectric too. That’s when they brought me in. Before my work in the U.S., you know, I studied with Paul Langevin in Paris, at the* École de Physique et Chimie*…Anyway, I tested them. Unlike quartz, their transmissible frequencies were essentially infinite. With prototypes I mapped not only the ocean floor, but also its subsurface and— beyond.”*

*“Beyond?”*

*“I saw maps of things I did not understand. I saw impossible folds in material structures, truths I never imagined…”*

*She trails off and looks dreamily at the black bar of Devil Reef.*

*“The potential applications are astounding. Diagnostic analysis in multiple fields. Extradimensional maps of staggering precision. Weapons.”*

*“So that’s it,” you say. “That’s why the agency’s so interested in Innsmouth.”*

*“Well, the Order’s supernatural and criminal activities* did *warrant a federal investigation. I came in later. But yes,” says Elina. “Now you know everything. That’s it.”*
